BECHKY   Transformation   of Understanding   on a Production   Floor  Managers should recognize that multiple understandings exist across occupational communities and find ways to promote the interaction   that would   allow such   under- standings to move and broaden the knowledge of differ- ent communities. The findings at EquipCo suggest that a strong focus on formal routines and procedures such as engineering drawings   might be detrimental   to problem   solving in organizations. Managers should consider providing and supporting   channels   for   communication   and   concrete solutions alongside formal processes. While engineers' design activities and assemblers' building activities are vital, organizations should encourage each occupational community to gain an understanding of the others' work, such as providing incentives to engineers to put on a bunny   suit   and   head   into   the production   area.   Simi- larly, instead of holding meetings in a distant   confer- ence room, project teams of engineers and assemblers should meet around the product to allow them a phys- ical   referent   to use   in   their interactions.   Augmenting formal   training regarding organizational   standards and processes (which tend to be expressed abstractly) with concrete visual aids would further encourage these con- crete communicative practices. Similarly,   these   findings   imply   that   organizations which   implement   technology-mediated   work   practices such as

telecommuting or virtual teams should consider how their groups are going to communicate and solve problems. If a cross-functional   team is meeting via a conference call, for example, my research at EquipCo would suggest that there will be many unresolvable ver- bal misunderstandings. Depending on the occupational groups involved and how much work context they share, meeting   physically   in   a setting   that   would   allow   for shared understanding of work objects might be a more efficient way to communicate across the team.  Conclusion  This study described the process by which understanding is transformed   across   occupational   communities,   gen- erating richer understandings   of the product   and pro- duction   process   within   the   organization.   Looking   in a   grounded   way   at   the   process   of   transformation   at EquipCo   uncovered   the   actions   that   workers   take   to make   organizationwide   learning   possible   and   demon- strated that simple transfer is not a good metaphor for such actions. A close examination   of the practices of occupational communities illustrated the significance of local work context in the transformation of understand- ing in organizations. The purpose   of   studying   the production   process   at EquipCo from an ethnographic perspective was to dis- cover   the   ways by   which   understanding   spread   from within occupational   communities   to others   throughout the organization. In this setting, t

he machine worked as a tangible definition to transform understandings, in part because the three groups had a similar enough context as a starting point. In some ways, this similarity meant that the groups were even less thoughtful about their dif- ferences. On the other hand, the similarity most likely allowed for easier creation of common ground. This sug- gests that these findings may not generalize to cross- occupational settings where the groups are less similar. In other settings, occupational communities may have to find other means for creating common ground. For instance, future research should consider whether different understandings exist in production settings that are organized   into cross-functional   teams. Since these teams regularly expose individuals to members of other occupational   groups,   the   understandings   of   the   team members may incorporate elements of the work of oth- ers, which would result in the need for different types of transformation. Similarly, how are understandings nego- tiated among nontechnical occupations? Examining the cross-occupational interactions in organizations outside of the manufacturing   realm would give further   insight into the knowledge transformation process. Finally, approaching the study of knowledge in organi- zations from a perspective that suggests that knowledge is local and develops through situated action reminds us that meaning in organizations is heterogeneous. Given that we each construct our unders

tanding of the world on the basis of our experience and interaction in it, the constructions we create will be different, and sometimes unclear to others. It will take some work to reconcile these differences. events.subject: research-question
events.statement: Gleanline split its paid subscription boxes from its free referred boxes precisely to protect the free side, yet within a year staff were describing the free households in the paid side's vocabulary: units, churn, conversion. Why did the separation move the money and not the language?

events.reason: The paper's central claim is precisely that structural separation of the kind Gleanline enacted does not by itself prevent one logic's norms from colonizing the other, which speaks directly to their puzzle.

events.subject: context
events.statement: Gleanline is a food-rescue community interest company in a Fenland market town. It collects supermarket surplus and packs it into weekly boxes. About 420 households pay nine pounds a week for a box; about 150 households referred by the food bank, a GP surgery or a school get the same box free. In 2024 the board merged the two packing lines so the free boxes stopped getting the bruised produce, and at the same time kept the teams apart: subscriptions and referrals never share a meeting except the Thursday pricing meeting. What made me want to study it is that the wall between the teams held, the produce got fairer, and the words did not hold. Within a year the referral coordinator was calling the households she exists for "units" in that meeting, and hating it on the stairs afterwards.

events.question: Which part of that is something you observed, and which part is something you were told?
events.reason: You write both in the same voice, and they carry very different weight.

events.text:
The Thursday field note gives you Rosa saying "units" in the room, in real time, which is one kind of ground. But the stairs quote, the "I hate that I said units" line, and Rosa's whole account of why "households" lasted a month, those come to you after the fact, in her retelling. Priya's "the sheet is what we look at every Thursday" is likewise her interpretation of why the language spreads, not something you watched spread.

Which part of that is something you observed, and which part is something you were told?

Observed: Dan asking about "conversion on the referral side", Marcus writing "referral units: 152" under "cost centre", nobody objecting, and Rosa using "units" herself twenty minutes later. I was in the room for all of that on 14 May. Told: the stairs line was said to me directly but it is her account of her own feeling; the month of "households" and the merged-line history come from her and Priya's retellings; Priya's claim that the sheet is what everyone looks at is her theory of the spread. So the migration itself I have seen once, in one meeting. The mechanism I have only been told. I have the Slack export and a year of board papers still to read, which should let me watch the vocabulary move over time rather than take their word for it.

events.title: 14 May meeting: Dan, Marcus, Rosa exchange on vocabulary
events.body: You were in the room and saw this directly: Dan asked about "conversion on the referral side," Marcus wrote "referral units: 152" under "cost centre," nobody objected, and twenty minutes later Rosa used "units" herself. This is the one instance of the vocabulary migration you have actually witnessed happening, in real time, in one meeting.

events.title: Migration evidence is one witnessed instance; earlier history is testimony
events.body: The migration itself you have seen once, in one meeting on 14 May. Everything before and around that (the "households" month, the merged-line history, the stairs comment) came to you as other people's retellings of their own experience or feeling, not things you watched happen. You have the Slack export and a year of board papers still unread, which should let you check whether the pattern holds over time rather than relying on their accounts of it.

events.title: Priya's claim that the sheet is "what everyone looks at"
events.body: Priya's explanation for why the vocabulary spread the way it did, that the sheet is the thing everyone looks at, is her theory of the mechanism, not something you observed. You don't yet have a way to tell whether that's actually what's driving it or just her account of it.

events.subject: site
events.statement: Gleanline is the right place because the separation was deliberate and recent. The board built the wall in 2024 on purpose, wrote down why, and I can date when each word crossed it: the Slack export runs from before the merged line, and the board papers are twice a year. Most hybrids drift without anyone having drawn the line first, so you cannot tell whether the line failed or never existed. Here the line exists on the org chart and I can watch the language ignore it. It is also small enough that one Thursday meeting is where the two sides meet, so the crossing has a room and a time. What it will be bad at showing: whether the vocabulary changes what the referral households actually get. The produce got better, the cap was set in a sentence about cost centres, and I cannot see inside a household. It is also one town and one grant, so anything about funders is thin. And I am not there on the days the referrals coordinator talks to the GP surgery, which may be where her own language lives.

events.subject: process
events.statement: The process is a word crossing the wall. One instance runs from the first time a term from the paid side is used about the free side in a shared setting, through the moment someone on the free side uses it about their own work, to the point where it appears in a document the free side authors, like Rosa's letter to the GP surgery or the board paper. For "units" that took about a year: it arrived with the merged line in 2024 as a cell in Marcus's sheet, was said aloud in meetings by spring 2025, and Rosa used it about her own list by May 2026. I also want to follow the rarer reverse crossing, "referral ends" replacing "lapses" on Dan's side and "the purpose the subscriptions serve" reaching the board paper, which seem to take longer and to travel through documents rather than meetings.

events.subject: outcome
events.statement: The outcome I care about is which vocabulary the free side ends up deciding in, because that is where the next decision about the free households comes from. The cap of 160 was decided in a sentence about cost centres, not in a sentence about families. So the outcome is not the words themselves but the terms of the next decision: whether a referral household is something you add or something you afford. I will know the outcome has moved when a decision about the referral list is argued entirely in the paid side's terms and nobody in the room notices, as happened on 14 May, or when the reverse holds and the board approves something because of what the free households are for. Produce quality is a second outcome I can see and it went the other way, which is part of the puzzle: the free side got better goods and worse words at the same time.

events.subject: sample
events.statement: The sample has to contain words that crossed and words that did not, in both directions. On the paid-to-free side I have "units", "churn", "conversion" and "cost centre"; I need at least one paid-side term that was said in the room and never taken up, so that the crossing is not just what happens to every word. On the free-to-paid side I have "referral ends" and "the purpose the subscriptions serve", and I need free-side terms that were offered and dropped, which Rosa's "households" gives me. The sample also has to contain the two channels, meetings and documents, because my hunch is that direction and channel go together. People: the four who sit in the Thursday meeting, the two volunteers who pack, and two board members, because the board paper is where the free side's sentence landed. Fourteen interviews so far, all staff and board; I have no referral households and no subscribers, which is a limit I should say out loud rather than pretend the sample covers them.

events.subject: bind
events.statement: Rosa's bind. If she speaks about the referral households as families in the Thursday meeting, she has not answered the question that was asked and she loses the argument, and the households lose the produce or the places. If she speaks about them as units she wins the argument and the households get the produce, and the next decision about them is made in a language in which they are a cost. She cannot protect them and describe them at the same time. The organisation's bind is the same one bigger: the wall that keeps the commercial team away from the free side is also what keeps the free side's words out of the room where money is decided, because the only shared thing is the sheet. Keep the wall and the sheet speaks for the free side. Take down the wall and the commercial team is in the referral work. Neither move gets the free side its own words in the room.

events.title: Referral coordinator's own language shifts despite deliberate wall
events.body: The board built a structural "wall" so the commercial side could not eat the charitable side, separate staff, Dan never touching referrals, Rosa never seeing a price [[chunk:56bb8424-84c8-4327-88ac-0e4523086f98]]. Yet Rosa finds herself using "units," the finance/subscription term, even though she says she hates it and it isn't how anyone actually thinks about the referral households [[chunk:46dd44b0-902c-4ad7-8bc4-5446cc240320]]. The wall holds organizationally but not linguistically, and that gap is unaccounted for.

events.title: Language crosses the wall in only one direction, mostly
events.body: Rosa observes that finance's terms reach the referral side every week via the spreadsheet, while referral language reaches finance only twice a year via the board paper, "the wall leaks both ways, but not equally" [[chunk:7ada3ea9-f18a-4e35-bbe5-c3d847e0c29a]]. The frequency of the shared artifact (weekly Thursday meeting, weekly spreadsheet) versus the biannual board paper appears to drive this asymmetry, but the material doesn't fully explain why frequency alone determines directionality.

events.title: Capacity decision made inside a cost-centre sentence
events.body: Rosa notes that "the cap at 160 was decided in a sentence about cost centres" [[chunk:7ada3ea9-f18a-4e35-bbe5-c3d847e0c29a]], and the fieldnote shows Marcus writing "referral units: 152" under a "cost centre" heading with no objection from anyone present, followed by the price/cap decision minutes later [[chunk:7e2396a9-09ad-4304-9543-5bb69b3530bd]] [[chunk:fbd23d47-c50b-41c7-bf2f-dca81a973787]]. It is unclear how a numeric/financial framing came to settle a question about referral capacity that the programme exists to serve.

events.title: Merged packing line eliminated 2023 produce quality gap
events.body: The board paper states the merged packing line "removed the produce quality gap between paid and referral boxes reported in 2023" [[chunk:43ee2363-f487-4bb9-9557-9646f7ff4751]]. You've distinguished the migration you watched from the mechanism you were told about, which is useful groundwork, but it doesn't yet tell me why the coupling/drift expectation is the wrong shape for what you've got rather than just an under-specified one. A contradiction needs the paper's expectation to predict something specific enough that Gleanline could have gone the other way and didn't, or gone the predicted way and didn't.

What, in the 14 May transcript, the board paper, or Rosa and Priya's accounts, is the case where the expectation would have predicted one outcome and you got a different one?

The anchor expectation predicts that where the anchor is strong the core stays put and drift is confined to the margins. At Gleanline the anchor is as strong as it gets: the board paper of 28 April opens its referral section with "the referral programme remains the purpose the subscriptions serve", Rosa's own sentence. The same page then prices each referral box as "a fully costed unit at £7.40" and proposes "a further 45 referral units". So the anchor sentence and the drifted vocabulary sit in one document, three lines apart, and the decision the document asks for, the cap at 160, is argued in the drifted terms. That is not the margins, that is the capacity decision about the people the anchor names. Second source: the 14 May field note, where "referral units: 152" goes on the whiteboard under "cost centre", nobody objects, and Rosa uses "units" herself within twenty minutes. Third source: Priya's interview, where the finance model gives every free box a revenue column with a zero in it, so the sheet itself renders the free households as paid boxes that do not pay. Three documents, three different authors, same deviation. What could have gone the other way and did not: the board could have written the capacity line in Rosa's terms, and Rosa could have kept "households" past a month.

That's three independently authored traces converging on the same deviation, which is a stronger design than most single-document contradictions get. But the anchor expectation isn't a single claim, it's a conditional: strong anchor confines drift to the margins. You've shown the drift reaching the capacity decision itself. What I don't yet have from you is whether that's the whole expectation failing or only half of it.

What in your setting fits this expectation, and what breaks it?

What fits: the wall on the org chart is exactly a formal coupling to the social-welfare demand, referrals reporting through Rosa and never seeing a price, and the informal frames drifted to the commercial side just as Pache and Santos say, with "units" and "churn" becoming the idiom of the only shared meeting. What breaks it: two things. First, the drift did not run through practices or people, it ran through an artefact. The sheet was built once by a part-time finance person and it does the drifting every Thursday; the people who use the words dislike them. Selective coupling expects the drift to sit in what people do informally, not in a spreadsheet nobody chose. Second, the direction is not simply toward the dominant or better-resourced logic. The referral side won the produce argument, won a cap rather than a cut, and got its sentence into the board paper. It lost the vocabulary and won the outcomes, which their account does not predict. Where the expectation stops holding here: their enterprises faced two external institutional demands; Gleanline faces one funder and one market, and the pressure that moved the words came from inside, from the merged line. So I would say it holds for the formal side and fails for the mechanism.

events.title: Drift running through an artefact nobody chose, not through practice
events.body: Selective coupling as you've been using it expects the drift to sit in what people do informally, in habits and interpretive frames that shift toward whichever logic is dominant. Here the drift runs through the sheet: it was built once by a part-time finance person and it does the drifting every Thursday, on its own, while the people who actually use "units" and "churn" dislike the words. That's not a variant of the expected mechanism, it's a different mechanism doing the same job, and I don't think the account as stated predicts an artefact that outlives and outworks the preferences of everyone who touches it.

events.title: Losing the vocabulary but winning the outcomes
events.body: The account that says the more legible logic's language migrates in expects that migration to travel with influence, the side that sets the terms should also be setting the results. But the referral side lost the words and still won the produce argument, got a cap instead of a cut, and got its own sentence into the board paper. Vocabulary dominance and outcome dominance came apart here, and I don't have an account that predicts they'd separate like that.

Battilana and Dorado expect that splitting the commercial and social-welfare work into separate structures will not stop the commercial logic's norms and vocabulary spreading into the social side unless who is hired and how they are socialised is also managed. What fits: the vocabulary did spread and the wall did not stop it, which is their claim exactly, and it is what the board was afraid of when it built the wall. What breaks it is the unless clause. Their microfinance banks lost the mission when the commercial staff won; here nobody won and the words moved anyway. Scope: their organisations hired from two worlds and had to socialise each into the other. Gleanline's staff came from one world, the town, and were split by task, so the workforce lever they rely on had nothing to pull on.

The second Bechky expectation, that a codified routine speaks the language of whoever codified it and others must adopt it to take part, fits the finance model exactly. In the field note of 14 May Marcus writes referral units: 152 on the whiteboard under cost centre and Rosa uses units herself twenty minutes later; in her interview of 21 May Priya says the sheet gives every free box a revenue column with a zero in it, and that you cannot argue with Marcus in the language of families. What breaks it is only the claim about who benefits: nobody at Gleanline codified the routine to gain from it, and the free side has won its arguments in the borrowed language.
